facts.claim: "Rock Bottom" is track 2 on Unholy Hymns by Bridge City Sinners, released August 20, 2021, and runs 3:34.

The album credits say all songs were written by the Bridge City Sinners. The album was engineered and produced by band fiddler Lightnin' Luke. Jesse Payne engineered and mixed it at LowShelf Recording in Portland, OR. Kris Crummett mastered it at Interlace Audio in Portland.
The album lineup is Libby Lux (lead vocals, banjolele), Michael Sinner (resonator guitar), Lightnin' Luke (fiddle), Clyde McGee (banjo) and Scott Michaud (upright bass).
Backing vocals on "Rock Bottom" were sung by Connor O'Neal, Shawn D'Amario and Spencer Mode of Tejon Street Corner Thieves.
"Rock Bottom" and "Pick Your Poison" were the first two singles from Unholy Hymns, which was set for release on Flail Records and SBÄM Records.
The band says they wrote Unholy Hymns during the pandemic, locked in bassist Scott's house together for three weeks.

The first half of the album, "Book I", is built on the band's dark but playful folk and jazz roots. It adds heavier subject matter such as addiction and mental health. "Rock Bottom" sits in this half.
Thoughts Words Action called "Rock Bottom" an unusually emotional song for the band. It said the violin and Libby's vocals make it stand out.
Saving Country Music compared the songwriting of "Rock Bottom" to Hank Williams and Townes Van Zandt. It also called the band one of the most successful gothic country acts.

Libby Lux said the band released Unholy Hymns on their own and that it charted on Billboard. She said their friend Jesse recorded it at Low Shelf Recording in Portland. She added that he used to play guitar in the band when it was a busking act.

Lead singer Libby Lux and bassist Scott Michaud were busking musicians who formed the band in 2016. They mixed string music with Prohibition-era jazz and ragtime and added a punk attitude. Unholy Hymns is the band's third album.

research.lineage: The Portland, Oregon band sits in a dark folk-punk and gothic country string-band tradition, blending Prohibition-era jazz and Appalachian "death folk" with punk DIY culture.

draft:
Every verse of **Rock Bottom** opens by calling a feeling by name, like an old acquaintance at the door: Lonely, Depression, Guilty, Regret, Hopeless, Drinking. The Bridge City Sinners treat despair as company. The song asks loneliness to hold on and say it loves them, while admitting that the love is a lie. Depression gets the warmest welcome of all: "Depression, hello, my old friend." The greeting is affectionate, even relieved, because at least with this friend nobody dies alone. That's the hard part to sit with. The narrator isn't fighting these feelings. They've moved in, and they're the only ones who stay.

The chorus works the same way. "There ain't no rock bottom for me" could be a boast or a confession, and Libby Lux sings it so it lands as both. The rest of the self-portrait shifts between moods. Guilt is a weight too heavy for anyone else to carry, which is half generosity and half pride. Regret turns into a shrug and a cigarette. The drinking verse ends on a question every relapse knows, about what anyone was thinking when they reached for the bottle again. None of it settles. The self-blame and the self-pity sit side by side.

Then the song ends on its real punchline. After the "oh"s pile up and the refrain repeats, the last line finally gives up the floor: "Rock bottoms only six feet deep." The only bottom is a grave. Saving Country Music compared the writing here to Hank Williams and Townes Van Zandt, and you can hear that plain, bone-dry way of looking at death head-on.

What makes it sting is the setting. The music is a lively shuffle. Upright bass walks underneath, a banjo runs fast, a guitar strums, and a fiddle sings over the top. The room sounds live and unpolished, like the band is playing a corner rather than a studio. Lux's voice is clear with a little rasp, steady and melodic rather than ragged. It's the band's busking roots, a mix of Prohibition-era string music and punk attitude, now carrying heavier weight. The band wrote *Unholy Hymns* during the pandemic, locked in bassist Scott Michaud's house for three weeks. They placed this song in the album's first half, where their dark, playful folk and jazz side takes on addiction and mental health. Thoughts Words Action called it unusually emotional for the band and singled out the fiddle and Lux's vocals. Three members of Tejon Street Corner Thieves add backing vocals, which turns the final chant into something closer to a barroom chorus than a lone confession.

The song lets you tap your foot while someone tells you, cheerfully and without flinching, that the only floor left is the one you get buried under.

factCheck.claim: "There ain't no rock bottom for me" and Libby Lux sings it.
factCheck.note: The quote matches. Lux as vocalist on this song is supported by the Thoughts Words Action coverage of her vocals.

factCheck.note: Reading of the lyrics, grounded in the text.

factCheck.claim: The last line is "Rock bottoms only six feet deep." It comes after the 'oh's and the refrain.
factCheck.note: The quote matches, and the lyric order shows it is the final line.
